slides.heading: Validate Bst
slides.subtitle: AlgoExpert · Medium · Binary Search Trees
slides.narration: Let's solve Validate Bst, a medium binary search trees problem. We'll restate the problem, build the intuition, walk through the approach, read the Java solution, and finish with its complexity.

slides.heading: The problem
bullets: Every node must be strictly greater than all left-subtree values and <= all right-subtree values.
slides.narration: Here's the problem. Every node must be strictly greater than all left-subtree values and under equals all right-subtree values.

slides.heading: Intuition
bullets: Every node must lie within bounds inherited from its ancestors, not just compared with its parent.
slides.narration: Every node must lie within bounds inherited from its ancestors, not just compared with its parent.

slides.heading: Brute force vs optimal
bullets: Naive: compare each node only with its children — WRONG
In-order traversal must be sorted → O(n)
Bounds passed down → O(n), early exit
slides.narration: The tempting mistake is to compare each node only with its direct children, which misses violations deeper down. Either check that in-order traversal is sorted, or pass down bounds inherited from all ancestors, which lets us stop at the first violation.

slides.heading: Approach
bullets: 1. Start with minus and plus infinity
2. Check the node is within bounds
3. Left child tightens the upper bound
4. Right child tightens the lower bound
slides.narration: Step by step. First, start with minus and plus infinity. Second, check the node is within bounds. Third, left child tightens the upper bound. Fourth, right child tightens the lower bound.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: 10 must be in [-∞, ∞) → ok
slides.narration: Node 10 must be at least -∞ and less than ∞. It is, so we continue.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: 5 must be in [-∞, 10) → ok
slides.narration: Node 5 must be at least -∞ and less than 10. It is, so we continue.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: 15 must be in [10, ∞) → ok
slides.narration: Node 15 must be at least 10 and less than ∞. It is, so we continue.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: 8 must be in [10, 15) → INVALID
slides.narration: Node 8 must be at least 10 and less than 15. It isn't: eight is in ten's right subtree, so the tree is not a valid BST.

slides.heading: Java solution
slides.narration: Valid returns true for null. It fails if the value is below the minimum or at least the maximum. Then it recurses left with the max tightened to the node's value, and right with the min raised to it.

slides.heading: Complexity
slides.narration: Time is O of n. Space is O of h.

slides.heading: Edge cases & pitfalls
bullets: Duplicates go right: left bound inclusive
Use long bounds for Integer.MIN/MAX values
slides.narration: The classic bug is a grandchild that's fine relative to its parent but violates an ancestor. Duplicates go right, and long bounds handle extreme integer values.

slides.heading: Interview tips & follow-ups
bullets: Follow-up: fix a BST with two swapped nodes (Repair BST)
slides.narration: Draw a counterexample for the naive approach before coding. The hard follow-up repairs a BST with two swapped nodes.

slides.heading: Recap
bullets: Every node must lie within bounds inherited from its ancestors, not just compared with its parent.
slides.narration: To recap Validate Bst: Every node must lie within bounds inherited from its ancestors, not just compared with its parent. Try re-implementing it from scratch without looking.
